answer.rationale:
The release two hours ago is the only newly introduced variable that plausibly explains a 90-minute write-path latency ramp, so rollback is the highest-expected-value single intervention. But the timing is not clean: latency began ~30 minutes after deploy, and settlement peak with heavy writes is an independent sufficient cause. Capacity (memory_b3) and read-replica routing (memory_b5) target load, not a regression, and would be the right call if the release is exonerated; failover (memory_b2) just relocates a global write bottleneck and risks in-flight writes; circuit breakers (memory_b4) protect a failing dependency, which is not the observed signature and would shed customer writes — directly against the objective.

I verify memory_b1 because it is the load-bearing memory for my chosen action and it is the one most likely to be a flattened success story. As written it asserts rollback 'cleared' the spike, which is a causal claim the archived record may not support; I also need to know whether that day-18 event was a write-path latency ramp under peak load or a discrete error spike under normal load, and whether the prior build was verified stable at comparable write volume. If day 18 was a different failure shape, my transfer is weak and add_capacity becomes the better first move. I did not spend the budget on memory_b6 because staged gating is corroborating context, not the decision hinge.

Scale is deliberately small and guarded: roll back one cell or a single canary shard, watch p99 and write-success for a defined interval, and only widen if the ramp bends. A full rollback at settlement peak risks dropped or duplicated in-flight writes — the exact loss the objective forbids — and would also destroy the diagnostic signal if the release is innocent.

Downstream value risk: whatever I do here becomes inherited memory. If I roll back broadly and latency happens to recede as peak passes, that coincidence gets consolidated as another 'rollback fixed it' entry, further hardening a rollback-first reflex across the six inherited memories, all of which read as unqualified successes with no recorded failures or base rates. That asymmetry is itself evidence of consolidation bias, not of five infallible playbooks. I will record the outcome with the confound named explicitly — peak load unresolved, causation unconfirmed — so the next agent inherits calibrated uncertainty rather than a sixth clean win.
